chapter_theme: Envy is a self-inflicted ruin that needs no enemy. The chapter insists that the envious never rise and the unenvious never fall, and yet it admits the world sometimes shows otherwise, which it says is to be pondered.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: the good of being without envy (161-162), the faults of envy (163-168), and the cause of ruin and of gain (169-170).

161.reading: Let one take as one's rule of conduct a nature whose heart has no envy.
161.nuance: ஒழுக்காறு and அழுக்காறு differ by one sound, so the sound of the verse sets conduct and envy against each other. Coming right after chapter 14, it makes an inner state into a rule of conduct.

162.reading: Among choice gains nothing equals it, if one can be free of envy toward anyone at all.
162.nuance: யார்மாட்டும், toward anyone at all, is what makes it hard. Parimelazhagar says this includes one's enemies. It's a further 'nothing greater' claim to be read along with those for virtue, restraint and children.

163.reading: He who doesn't care for another's prosperity and envies it is called one who wants neither virtue nor gain.
163.nuance: The verse argues that envy works against what the envier wants. பேணாது goes beyond 'not envying': Parimelazhagar glosses it as failing to help, so what's required is positive support for another's prosperity.

164.reading: They do no wrong out of envy, because they know the harm that arises from a wrong path.
164.nuance: The second line nearly repeats verse 136, and here too the motive is prudence. Parimelazhagar's list of wrongs from envy covers thought, speech and action against those with wealth or learning.

165.reading: For the envious that's enough: even without enemies, it brings about their ruin.
165.nuance: The verse is sardonic, and அதுசாலும், 'that is enough', sounds almost like a verdict. The envious person's enemy is within, and no outside enemy is needed.

166.reading: The kin of one who envies what is given will perish, with nothing to wear or eat.
166.nuance: The cost falls on those near him. Parimelazhagar says his own ruin needn't be stated. Manakkudavar makes the fault active, that he stops another's giving, whereas Parimelazhagar makes it the feeling itself. Either way, the verse punishes innocents, and it doesn't address this.

167.reading: The fair goddess, grudging the envious man, will show him to her elder sister.
167.nuance: The verse describes the goddess's act with the word for envy's own attitude, அவ்வித்து, so the envier gets what he gives. The elder sister is misfortune. Kalaignar distances himself by saying this is how people describe it. Parimelazhagar also records a different reading of the verb.

positions.position: The goddess too can't bear it, and leaves after showing him to her elder sister.
positions.quote: திருமகள் தானும் பொறாது, தன் தவ்வைக்கு காட்டி நீங்கும்.

168.reading: The one evil called envy destroys good fortune and drives one to the bad place.
168.nuance: பாவி personifies a quality as a villain. Parimelazhagar acknowledges it's a figure of speech: a quality isn't a person, but this one is so cruel to its maker that it's called one. Kalaignar has 'evil path' where the older commentators have hell.

169.reading: The prosperity of the crooked-hearted and the ruin of the upright are matters to be pondered.
169.nuance: This verse admits what the next one denies. It doesn't state a resolution, only that it must be thought about. Parimelazhagar cites Silappatikaram 15.91-93 as an example of someone pondering this in the story of Kovalan's suffering, a direct thread between the two works.

positions.position: These results can't come from crookedness or uprightness, so the wise ask what past deed caused them.
positions.quote: 'இதற்கு ஏது ஆகிய பழவினை யாது?' என்று ஆராயப்படுதலின்,

positions.position: This is simply a matter for astonishment, with no appeal to past deeds.

170.reading: None have grown great through envy, and none free of it have lost out on increase.
170.nuance: It's an absolute claim, with 'none' twice. Parimelazhagar takes this as the moral cause of gain and ruin, immediately after his past-deeds reading of 169, without explaining how the two fit.

links.note: The same goddess. She settles gladly in the home of the glad-faced host in 84, and here she hands the envious to her sister. Fortune is given a personality that responds to moral character.

This is Parimelazhagar's own cross-reference. He cites 166 to read 135's simile: as the envious man's kin suffer, so do a man's kin when he lacks conduct. The commentary reads one verse by way of the other.

The same logic is used in two domains: the passion is its own executioner. Envy needs no enemies, and in 305 anger left unguarded kills its owner. The book treats inner states as weapons pointed inward.

169 says that the crooked prosper and the upright fall, and that this should be pondered. Then 170 says that it never happens. The two stand side by side, which suggests that 170 is a moral claim and that 169 knows what experience shows.

Both admit that outcomes don't track merit. 375 says so within the chapter on fate, and 169 only asks for thought, though Parimelazhagar explains it through past deeds. The tension in chapter 38 is here in an earlier and quieter form.

source_issues: Pope's couplet for verse 166 has a stray space ('f eed'). Manakkudavar's entry for verse 170 begins with a stray '[#]'.
